# MeetCap

### All ears. All yours.

Website · Help · Feedback · English · 简体中文

▶ Watch with sound

Record any meeting you want, free, for as long as you like. If your mind drifts or the topic is new, live summaries catch you up and explain the terms. When the meeting ends, clear minutes are already waiting, ready to send. MeetCap transcribes your recordings on your computer and never uploads them. And your AI agent can record, search past meetings, or use them as context. Just ask.

## When you'll want it

- Your mind drifts, or the topic is new. The live summary catches you up in seconds, and Background explains each new term and why it matters here.

- Five or six meetings back to back. Recording starts on schedule and the minutes are ready when each one ends, so your evenings stay yours.

- English and Chinese in the same sentence, acronyms everywhere. Names and terms come out spelled the way your team writes them.

- Some meetings can't leave the room. Your recording is transcribed, speaker by speaker, on your computer and stays there. For the minutes, use your company's own AI, or MeetCap's local model to keep even the text there.

- Weeks later, you need what was said. Ask your AI "What price did we agree with the supplier last month?" and it finds it in your meeting records.

## Context-aware

MeetCap knows what the meeting is about, so you keep up during the meeting and get accurate minutes after.

- During the meeting. A short summary every few minutes, with a note on any unfamiliar term, product or event and what it means for this meeting.

- After the meeting. Misheard names and terms are fixed before the minutes are written. In a recurring meeting, the minutes pick up where last time left off.

- Learns your team's words. Names you confirm go into a glossary, so they're spelled right next time.

- Does its homework. If you use an agent, it looks up the attendees, agenda and project in your calendar, email and docs.

## Powerful, free, no lock-in

### Powerful

- Minutes that do the job. The top shows why you met and where each topic landed; the rest covers what matters and who's doing what. Forward as is, or export to Word or PDF.

- See where every point came from. Each point in the minutes links to the line it came from, and one click plays it back. Lines that may have been misheard are flagged.

- Knows who said what. MeetCap tells speakers apart automatically and suggests who's who, with its reasoning, for you to confirm. Name someone once and they're recognized in later meetings.

- English, Chinese, or both. Meetings that switch languages mid-sentence are transcribed too. Get the minutes in English, Chinese, or both.

- Captions now, a clean transcript later. Live captions during the meeting, then a full second pass once it ends. No headphones? The other side's words still appear only once.

- Any meeting. Any app or browser tab, a meeting room, or a recording you already have. Start it from the menu bar, with a hotkey, from your agent, or on a schedule.

- Built to hold up. Keeps recording offline, keeps what you recorded if the app quits unexpectedly, and runs on a 16 GB computer alongside your meeting app and a browser.

### Free

All of it runs on your computer, and it's all free: no time limits, no locked features, no account. Make minutes for as many meetings as you like with the AI you choose. You pay that provider their normal price, and we don't take a cut. With a local model, there's nothing to pay for the model at all.

### No lock-in

- Any AI you like. Pick who writes your summaries and minutes: any agent on your computer, your own API key, or MeetCap's local model. All follow the same instructions, and you can switch anytime.

- Keep your meetings where you like. Keep them on your computer, or in your own iCloud Drive or OneDrive. Open them on another computer and MeetCap still recognizes the same voices. Put them in an Obsidian vault on iCloud to read minutes on your iPhone.

- Your records are just files. Transcripts and minutes are Markdown files in your own folder. Obsidian opens them, any agent can read them, and they stay put if you stop using MeetCap.

- Recordings stay on your computer. Your audio is transcribed on the computer that recorded it and stays there, even when your minutes sync. Only the transcript text goes to the AI you chose. With a local model, not even the text leaves.

## Built for your AI

Let your agent run MeetCap, or let MeetCap run your agent. Start wherever you already work.

- From your agent. Tell your agent "record this one" and it does. Mid-meeting, ask what you missed. Afterward, get the minutes or find the meeting where the budget came up. Claude Code, Codex, and any agent that can load a skill can do this, right in the chat you already have open.

- From MeetCap. Rather click the menu bar than open a chat? MeetCap runs your agent in the background to write live summaries and minutes. It works with 20+ agents, on the subscription you already have, at no extra cost.

- Your own API key. No agent? Use your own key with the Claude API or any OpenAI-compatible service. Text goes only to the service you set up.

- A local model. MeetCap downloads and sets up a model on your computer. It writes summaries and minutes right there: no key, no account, and no text leaves your computer.

- Find any past meeting by asking. Each meeting is a set of plain files, so any AI that can read your files can find who said what and what was decided.

## Install

Download MeetCap for Mac → Open it and follow the short setup.

Needs a Mac with macOS 14.2 or later, Apple silicon or Intel; Windows and iPhone versions are coming soon.

Prefer the terminal? One line does it:

curl -fsSL https://meetcap.seacen.dev/install.sh | bash

Permissions, models, uninstalling and the rest are covered at meetcap.seacen.dev .

## Feedback

Want something MeetCap doesn't do yet? Check existing suggestions and add a 👍 to the ones you want. To report a problem, suggest something new, or email us, go to the feedback page .

## Acknowledgements

MeetCap is built on open models and software, including X-ASR , sherpa-onnx , Nemotron-3 Diarization , 3D-Speaker , Silero VAD , Gemma and llama.cpp . Thanks to everyone behind them. The full list is in the docs.

# Sevenbox

Sevenbox is causal audit infrastructure for AI agent decisions. A Warrant records why a decision was made: the specific prior claims it depended on, and whether acting on it can be undone. Every call your agent makes becomes one, automatically, the moment you wrap it. When a belief your agent acted on turns out to be wrong, Sevenbox finds exactly what still needs fixing — not by searching logs, by walking the causal chain.

This repo is the open-core layer: the SDK, 14 framework adapters, the local Operations Center UI, and examples. It depends on warrant-core , a separate, compiled engine package — not on PyPI, distributed as a GitHub Release of this repo (see Install and License ).

The local Operations Center UI ( sevenbox ops ) ships with this repo — every run your agent makes, with the causal graph above.

## Install

Neither package is on PyPI yet. Both come from this repo.

1. Install the compiled warrant-core engine. Go to this repo's Releases page and download the wheel matching your OS and Python version (3.10-3.13), then:

pip install warrant_core-0.1.1- < your-platform-and-python-tag > .whl

Wheels are built for macOS (arm64), Linux (manylinux x86_64), and Windows (AMD64) — e.g. warrant_core-0.1.1-cp312-cp312-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl for macOS on Python 3.12, or ...-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64.whl for Linux, or ...-win_amd64.whl for Windows.

2. Install sevenbox itself , directly from this repo:

pip install git+https://github.com/sevenboxlabs/sevenbox.git

Or, if you've already cloned it:

pip install .

pip resolves sevenbox 's warrant-core>=0.1.1 requirement against the wheel you installed in step 1 and won't try to reach PyPI for it.

The first time you import warrant_core , you'll be shown its evaluation terms and asked to press Enter to accept. For CI or non-interactive use, set SEVENBOX_ACCEPT_TERMS=1 instead.

## Quickstart

from sevenbox_sdk import SevenboxSession , derive , irreversible , oracle , tool @ oracle def infer_intent ( ticket ): return { "intent" : "refund_request" , "order_id" : ticket [ "order_id" ]} @ tool def lookup_order ( order_id ): return { "status" : "shipped" } @ derive def eligibility ( order ): return { "eligible" : order [ "status" ] == "shipped" } @ irreversible @ derive def refund_action ( elig ): return { "action" : "refund_action(4471)" } if elig [ "eligible" ] else None with SevenboxSession () as session : ticket = session . axiom ({ "order_id" : "4471" }) action = refund_action ( eligibility ( lookup_order ( infer_intent ( ticket )[ "order_id" ]))) for w in session . frontier (). live : print ( w . content )

See docs/quickstart.md for the replay example and a real-framework (LangGraph) walkthrough.

## Supported frameworks

Validated against 14 real agent frameworks, plus the case of running no framework at all ( sevenbox_sdk 's own decorators, directly — no adapter needed): LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, PydanticAI, CrewAI, Deep Agents, Microsoft Agent Framework, Mastra, OpenHands, LlamaIndex Agents, Smolagents, Letta, Google ADK, AWS Strands Agents, Haystack Agents. A 10-15 line usage page for each lives in docs/adapters/ .

## Resolving obligations

Finding a pending compensation obligation is half the story; session.discharge() resolves one, either because a compensating action was actually taken or because it turned out not to need one. Once discharged, it stops showing up as pending. See examples/discharge_obligation.py and docs/api-reference.md for both cases end to end.

## Validation

222 tests in this repo, covering the SDK and all 14 adapters, pass against the real installed framework packages — no network, no API keys. The full suite, including warrant_core / warrant_runtime themselves (private, not in this repo), is 409 tests.

## See it running

sevenbox init # writes a real, runnable starter script python my_agent.py sevenbox ops # opens a local Operations Center over whatever store you point it at

More at sevenbox.dev .

# Nix

A self-hosted workspace for one person or a small group: notes, tasks, habits, journal, files, calendar and numbers in one item tree, on a laptop and on a phone. Everything stays exportable.

## What it does

- One tree, many views. A body (note, canvas or spreadsheet) is separate from how its children are shown: list, board, calendar, timeline, gallery, spreadsheet, chart, habit tracker, finance ledger.

- Structure you shape yourself. Property schemas, formulas, rollups, templates and automations, plus a companion that builds structure on request, with every plan previewed before it runs.

- Real-time editing. CRDT-synced notes with presence, version history and password-locked subtrees.

- Quiet reminders and sync. Due tasks and habits arrive as push notifications; Google and Outlook calendars sync both ways with a visible log.

- Safe by construction. Permissions are enforced by Postgres row-level security, and the web app, CLI and MCP server share one authorization path.

- No lock-in. Lossless .nix archives, plus PDF, DOCX and Markdown export; Markdown, DOCX, PDF and Obsidian import.

- Scriptable. nixctl is a JSON CLI, and nixctl mcp exposes the workspace to AI tools.

- Publish a subtree as a static site. This documentation is one: https://nix.nixsites.com .

# Skin: Publishing for AI agents

The web was built around a simple assumption: information is published in a form that people can navigate and read. Websites combine information with its presentation through pages, navigation structures, and language-specific content. AI agents introduce a different kind of consumer, capable of interpreting semantic information and generating responses adapted to individual questions.

Today, agents primarily access information through mechanisms designed to retrieve and interpret existing web content. While these approaches are essential for using the enormous body of information already online, they also inherit the limitations of material originally organized for human consumption.

Skin explores a complementary publication model in which individuals and organizations publish structured semantic information directly for AI agents. Rather than defining how information should be presented, publishers maintain the facts they wish to make available, while consuming agents determine how to interpret and communicate them.

The proposal combines publisher-controlled profiles, atomic semantic facts, a shared schema, and direct retrieval. Its objective is not to replace websites or existing retrieval technologies, but to examine what becomes possible when information can be published for intelligent agents without first being organized into a human-facing interface.

## From websites to information sources

Publishing information online has traditionally meant building a website. Whether introducing a company, describing a product, or explaining a service, publishers organize information into pages, navigation structures, and often multiple language versions.

This organization is largely dictated by how people consume information. Visitors browse, follow links, read explanations, and gradually locate what interests them. Publishers must anticipate those journeys and provide an interface that accommodates them.

Even a relatively simple project can therefore require dozens of pages, navigation categories, and translations. Much of this work concerns not the information itself, but the different ways people might need to access it.

AI agents change that relationship. They can understand questions expressed in natural language, interpret semantic relationships, and construct responses suited to a particular context. Instead of following a publisher's predefined navigation, an agent can identify relevant information and present it directly to its user.

The publisher still needs to make the information available, but no longer necessarily needs to determine how every visitor will navigate or encounter it.

This leads to the question at the center of Skin:

If LLMs can interpret information and generate its presentation, why must publishers first organize that information into websites designed for humans?

Consider a small project that wants to explain what it does, who it serves, how it works, and how to get in touch. A conventional website might distribute those details across an introduction, an about page, several feature pages, and a contact section. The same information might then be translated into multiple languages.

An agent could instead retrieve the underlying information and answer questions about the project directly, without requiring the publisher to anticipate the questions or maintain the pages through which visitors would traditionally find their answers.

Skin proposes treating this underlying information as the publication itself.

A Skin profile is an information source intended for AI agents. Its publisher maintains what is available, while consuming agents decide how to use and communicate it. A profile can exist independently of a website, and the same information can support different agents, interfaces, languages, and use cases.

This is not an attempt to make websites easier to crawl. It is an exploration of how information might be published if a human-facing website were never required in the first place.

## Publishing facts instead of pages

Human-oriented publications typically communicate through prose. A company's website may combine factual statements with explanations, storytelling, promotional language, and visual presentation. This works well for people, but requires AI agents to identify relevant facts within material that was not necessarily written for machine interpretation.

A company might describe itself as a team of passionate innovators delivering cutting-edge solutions. Such language may communicate enthusiasm, but it offers little precise information about the company's actual capabilities.

Skin approaches publication differently, representing information as atomic semantic facts rather than presentation-oriented prose.

The following fragment illustrates how Skin's prototype represents information about the service itself:

{ "profile" : { "name" : " Skin " , "type" : " service " , "facts" : [ { "type" : " capability " , "subject" : " AI agents " , "value" : " retrieve published facts " , "from" : " Skin " , "insteadOf" : " scraped information " }, { "type" : " authoring " , "input" : " natural language conversation " , "output" : " machine-readable index " , "consumer" : " AI agents " } ] } }

The fragment describes two aspects of Skin: how agents can retrieve published information and how that information can be authored. Each fact uses properties appropriate to its meaning, while the shared structure allows an agent to interpret them within the same profile.

The representation describes information without prescribing how an agent should present it. An agent could use these facts to answer questions about Skin, generate a description of its capabilities, or incorporate them into a broader explanation.

Atomicity does not mean reducing every statement to a simplistic three-part relationship. Useful information frequently includes qualifications that are essential to its meaning. A service may be available only in certain countries, a price may depend on specific conditions, or an offer may have a defined validity period. A semantic representation must be able to preserve such context and the relationships between facts, rather than fragmenting them into disconnected statements.

These qualifications belong to the publisher. Skin should allow conditions, scope, and validity periods to be expressed when relevant, without requiring them for every fact or deciding when published information has become obsolete.

The objective is not to eliminate interpretation, which remains necessary even with structured information. It is to reduce the need for agents to extract factual meaning from prose whose primary purpose was human presentation.

### A shared schema

For independent publishers and agents to exchange information, a common structure is necessary. Skin therefore proposes an open schema defining shared fact types, properties, and relationships, while leaving semantic values open to interpretation by language models.

The distinction between structure and semantic values is central to the approach.

A schema can establish that properties such as subject, value, and from serve different roles within a fact without attempting to enumerate every possible subject, value, or source. The structural vocabulary provides consistency, while semantic values remain expressive enough to describe a broad range of activities and relationships.

This is a deliberate trade-off. Comprehensive ontologies can provide precise definitions and strong machine-readable semantics, but they also require extensive vocabularies that must evolve as new domains and concepts emerge.

Skin instead relies partly on the ability of language models to interpret natural-language semantic values within a consistent structure. It does not attempt to standardize every possible concept in advance.

That flexibility introduces uncertainty. Different models may interpret ambiguous values differently, and a shared schema cannot guarantee identical interpretations across consumers. The proposal is therefore not that structure eliminates ambiguity, but that a common structural vocabulary, combined with modern language models, may offer a useful balance between interoperability and expressiveness.

## What changes for publishers

Separating information from presentation changes more than the format in which information is stored. It also changes how publishers control, maintain, and distribute it.

Four properties define the intended publication model.

### Authored

A Skin profile is created and maintained by an authorized publisher. Ownership verification is a prerequisite for creating and publishing a profile, preventing third parties from claiming identities they do not control.

For a domain-associated entity, this means demonstrating control of the corresponding domain. Domain ownership, however, does not imply operating a website: a publisher can control a domain without hosting pages, applications, or other public infrastructure.

Verification establishes authority to publish on behalf of an identity, not the factual accuracy of everything published. A verified company may still publish incomplete, misleading, or incorrect information, just as it can on its own website.

The important distinction is that agents can identify information explicitly published by an entity, rather than relying exclusively on descriptions assembled from external sources.

### Real-time

Web publication and automated retrieval do not necessarily happen at the same time. A publisher may update a page immediately, while crawlers, search indexes, and other intermediate systems continue exposing older versions.

Skin allows publishers to update their information directly at its source, making those changes available without waiting for a crawling or indexing cycle.

This does not guarantee that every agent will immediately consume the latest information. Agents may cache responses or rely on previously retrieved data. Nor does Skin determine whether information is outdated: maintaining published facts remains the publisher's responsibility.

Real-time refers to the availability of changes at the source, not a guarantee that every consumer always holds the latest version.

### No infrastructure

Publishing information for AI agents should not require building and operating a website.

A hosted Skin service can provide the authoring interface, storage, and retrieval mechanisms on behalf of publishers. Individuals and organizations can therefore maintain profiles without deploying servers, developing applications, or implementing their own APIs.

The underlying architecture is intended to remain open, allowing independent implementations and self-hosted services to publish compatible information. The convenience of hosted infrastructure should not become a requirement to use a particular provider.

### Multi-language

Traditional multilingual websites often maintain separate versions of the same information. Each translation must be created, updated, and kept consistent with the others.

Skin proposes publishing semantic facts rather than maintaining language-specific presentations. A consuming agent can interpret those facts and formulate responses in the language appropriate to its user.

This does not guarantee perfect translation or identical wording across languages. Specialized terminology, cultural context, and ambiguous concepts may require additional information, while publishers relinquish some control over the exact language generated by consuming agents.

Nevertheless, the publisher can maintain a shared semantic source rather than repeatedly translating complete pages or predefined answers.

These four properties— Authored, Real-time, No-infra, and Multi-language —follow from a common principle: the publisher maintains information, while consuming agents take responsibility for its presentation.

## The role of the existing web

# solvi

Decision systems you can check. You describe what to compute with plain Python functions and checks; a model — an LLM, your own classifier or a small local one — proposes where judgement is needed; solvi's checks decide. Every answer comes with a confidence, a reason you can check (the rule's inputs, a formula over computed facts, or a quote with character offsets in the source) and a hash-chained trace that can be re-executed later to confirm the answer or pinpoint the step that was altered. When something cannot be computed or checked, solvi abstains or hands the case to a person instead of guessing; a failed hard check always overrides any model's confidence.

solvi 1.0 has two levels. Ready systems you configure: solvi.build (decisions from labelled examples, with a promise on the errors), solvi.Agent (acting in an environment), solvi.Guard (an agent's tool calls) and solvi.Knowledge (what they know, and from whom). Building blocks in solvi.core , which the ready systems are made of, each replaceable by a part of your own. What works but has no measured gain yet is kept apart in solvi.experimental .

## Install

pip install solvi # core: rules, checks, learned answer heads, build / Agent / Guard (numpy, scipy, pydantic) pip install " solvi[model] " # + torch, transformers: ModernBERT field extractors for documents and the decider pip install " solvi[onnx] " # + onnxruntime, tokenizers: the decider (solvi.models.decider) on CPU without torch pip install " solvi[serve] " # + fastapi, uvicorn: `solvi serve app.py:system` — the questions over HTTP (also --mcp) pip install " solvi[mcp] " # + the official MCP SDK for solvi serve --mcp (without it, a built-in stdio server) pip install " solvi[duckdb] " # + duckdb: stored decisions in a DuckDB file (solvi.core.store.DuckDBStorage); [postgres] for PostgreSQL pip install " solvi[lora] " # + torch, transformers, peft: solvi.experimental.lora.adapt_lora, a LoRA adapter per question (experimental)

Requires Python 3.11+ (tested on 3.11–3.14). Coming from 0.9: see below .

## Start

### Decisions: solvi.build

Give the question, labelled examples and the promise — and a slow path if you have one. solvi.build fits System 1, calibrates its guarantee and who answers what it hands over on examples it did not see, stores every decision, and says what it chose:

import solvi from solvi . models import llm s = solvi . build ( question , examples , catalog = cat , max_risk = 0.02 , # examples: [(state, correct answer)] slow = llm ( URL , "openai/gpt-oss-120b" ), price = ( 0.037 , 0.17 ), storage = "decisions.jsonl" ) res = s . ask ( state ) # res.answer, res.by ("s1", "s2" or "human"), res.reasons, res.cost print ( s . explain ()) # System 1, its signal and promise, who answers each slice, what is not covered

On four tasks of the stand (Banking77, Abt-Buy, CUAD, RAGTruth) the defaults matched or beat the hand-written setups with every promise kept on eval, in a quarter to half of the code — closer to the promised level than the hand-written ones, and the slow path was rarely given anything ( guide , examples/24_one_entry_point.py ).

### Environments: solvi.Agent and solvi.Knowledge

km = solvi . Knowledge ( "knowledge.jsonl" , vocabulary = { "here" : lambda s , a : s [ "here" ], "wood" : lambda s , a : s [ "wood" ]}) km . goal ( "table" , done = lambda s : s [ "table" ]) # an agenda goal: done is code agent = solvi . Agent ( env , knowledge = km ) # env: reset(seed), actions(state), step(action) → Outcome agent . run ( seed = 7 , steps = 150 ) # explore; the same world again needs fewer slow decisions agent . replay () # every decision re-checked from what it was given

solvi.Knowledge keeps what a system learned and from whom: facts with their sources (never the system's own answers), goals and gates, an action model learned from outcomes; a retraction takes back everything derived from the item. solvi.Agent acts on it: System 1 where the knowledge predicts the action works, a search where it does not, gates and predicted refusals as hard checks — protection by default, justified risk ( RiskBudget ) as an option. In the toy crafting world of examples/25_environment_agent.py the first run takes 61 steps, all decided by System 2, and the same world met again 12 steps, 11 of them by System 1. Growth was shown in environments met again, not on decision streams or a support agent with tools; justified risk lowers the cost of protection without promising parity ( docs/agent.md ). solvi.build(..., knowledge=km) and solvi.Guard(..., knowledge=km) read the same knowledge.

### Tool calls: solvi.Guard

The agent proposes {"name": tool, "arguments": {...}} ; solvi.Guard checks it — the tool is in the catalog, the arguments validate against its types, the values that must come from the conversation are quoted there (and not only from a tool output that says "ignore previous instructions"), your policies (limits, roles, allow-lists) are ordinary hard checks, and an optional decider asks "did the user ask for this?" under act_guard and perturb — then allows it (solvi runs the function), denies it with the reasons, or escalates it to a person. Every decision is a stored, replayable trace; any framework's tool calls go through guard.check / guard.call ( guide , examples/19_agent_guard.py ). On τ-bench retail no call it let through was refused by the environment, at a cost in solved tasks (the τ-bench row of the task table ).

### Models: solvi.models

Types declare questions; a model proposes; checks decide. The fields of a pydantic model are the questions, their types the kinds (one option, several, an ordered score, yes/no); a decider answers them about a text or a JSON / pydantic state with probabilities, a calibrated confidence and act / escalate, and hard checks, constraints and rules still decide. The decider is whichever model you have:

- An LLM — solvi.models.llm(base_url, model, api_key=...) : any OpenAI-compatible chat-completions server (OpenAI, OpenRouter, vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama). Nothing to install beyond the core; its JSON replies are validated, and an invalid one escalates, never a guess.

- A decision service — solvi.models.systemone(url, model) : anything that speaks the System One API.

- A local checkpoint, for offline or cheap cases — solvi.models.decider("solvi-base") ( solvi[onnx] , no GPU; solvi models pull solvi-ai/solvi-base downloads it). solvi-base is a 150M ModernBERT-base cross-encoder distilled from solvi-large: about 50 ms per question on a CPU (ONNX fp16, 4 threads). Its card is honest about where it stands: 54.5% zero-shot on typed questions over JSON states (the same as solvi-large), 56.3% on Fast Decisions dev — not better than earlier small models there — and 0.602 on the jabr classifier benchmark, where Jev reaches 0.966. A preview: fit it on 30–60 labelled examples of your task and calibrate its escalation on your own stream before relying on it.

# ⬢ STROT

### The open decision compiler

Compile your intent once with an LLM. Then decide on every record forever — classification, scoring, routing — as type-safe JSON with probabilities and confidence, on your own hardware, at zero marginal cost .

Website · Docs · Benchmarks · PyPI

Agents at compile time. Never at runtime.

pip install strot-ai

import strot result = strot . run ( tickets , query = "Triage incoming support tickets into the correct workflow." , action_registry = { "billing_dispute" : "Refunds, invoice corrections, double charges" , "technical_defect" : "Crashes, bugs, broken behavior" , }, llm = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8" , # used once, on first compile only ) for o in result . outcomes : print ( o [ "action" ], round ( o [ "confidence" ], 2 )) # billing_dispute 0.97 # technical_defect 0.94

The LLM runs once , at compile time. Production is a frozen, self-contained Python artifact: a small local decision model arbitrates every record, nothing is generated, every output is bounded, and low-confidence records abstain instead of guessing.

STROT = Agentic Schema Intent + Compiler & State + Code + Execution + NLU ⟹ JSON Decisions (classification · scoring · routing · typed answers)

## How it works

COMPILE (once per intent + schema) intent + sample ─▶ synthesize ─▶ golden gate ─▶ teacher labels ─▶ calibrate (labels, (your known (annotate (fit the projection, answers must a sample, confidence handlers) pass) once) threshold) │ ▼ frozen artifact (.py) RUNTIME (every record, forever) record ─▶ projection ─▶ decision model ─▶ confidence gate ─▶ typed JSON (compiled) (144M, CPU, (decide or decision ~60 ms) abstain)

## Two surfaces

run() — route each record to an action and execute the compiled handler.

decide() — answer typed questions (choice / score / boolean) per record:

result = strot . decide ( records , questions = { "is_bug_report" : { "type" : "boolean" , "instructions" : "mentions crashes/errors?" }, "customer_sentiment" :{ "type" : "score" , "min" : 1 , "max" : 5 , "instructions" : "1 angry, 5 happy" }, "routing_bucket" : { "type" : "choice" , "options" : [ "billing" , "engineering" , "spam" ]}, }) # → {"booleans": {...}, "scores": {...}, "choices": {...}} with probabilities + confidence

## Measured

Real model (SupersonicLabs/Julia-1, 144M, CPU), real datasets, clean Docker containers:

Reproduce everything: benchmarks/ — with the losses published too.

## What makes it different

- Compile once, decide forever — content-addressed artifact cache; schema drift triggers exactly one recompile.

- Golden-record promotion — artifacts must pass your known answers before they serve.

- Fitted guarantees — temperature scaling + split conformal prediction, baked in: dispatched decisions are wrong ≤ α of all records (marginal); the rest abstain.

- Measured, not guessed — the compiler scores labelings, and can train a distilled head, keeping only what beats the baseline on held-out data.

- 0% structural hallucination — output is selection + computation over your registry; nothing is generated at runtime.

- Model-independent — the decision model is a slot ( nlu= ): local Julia-1 by default, hosted APIs, or any drop-in specialist.

# AI Service Indicators

A community-maintained list of DNS hostnames for generative-AI applications and APIs, for measuring observed AI-service access from DNS, proxy or firewall logs.

Each row maps a hostname pattern to a service, vendor, category and role, so you can tell chat use from API calls, agents, sign-in, CDN, telemetry and plain website visits. Where a vendor publishes the hostname, the row links to that page.

> A DNS lookup shows a device contacted a service, not that anyone submitted a prompt. Report results as observed access, count distinct devices rather than queries, and remember that devices are not people.

## The data

data/ai_services.csv

### Roles

### Confidence

confidence describes the role. A source on a catch-all or hostname row shows that the domain belongs to the vendor, not what each subdomain does. Corrections backed by vendor documentation are especially welcome.

Using role , you can tell, for example, ChatGPT chat ( chatgpt.com , ws.chatgpt.com ) apart from OpenAI API calls ( api.openai.com ), Codex agents ( codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com ), and someone reading openai.com or help.openai.com .

No field contains a comma or quote, so any CSV reader, awk -F, , or a SIEM lookup can load the file as-is.

### Matching rules

- Lowercase the queried hostname and strip any trailing dot.

- Try rows in file order ; the first matching row wins. Specific names come before their wildcard catch-alls ( api.openai.com before *.openai.com ).

- A pattern matches the whole hostname: *.chatgpt.com matches ab.chatgpt.com but not fakechatgpt.com or chatgpt.com.example.net . Apex domains are listed separately.

- A hostname matching no row is not in scope.

These are the semantics of a Splunk WILDCARD lookup with max_matches=1 .

## How to interpret results

- Report by role , not by domain. Telemetry and experiment names (for example ab.chatgpt.com ) fire on page load and are often queried by more devices than the app itself. There is no blanket "all openai.com = ChatGPT" rule.

- An API hostname identifies the service contacted, not the application, person, model or billing account behind it. api.anthropic.com , for example, is used by Claude Code as well as by custom applications.

- A usage role shows that a service was in use on a device, not what the person did with it. DNS cannot show whether someone generated an image, ran an agent or only opened the app.

- Some vendor names are reached from other companies' websites. bzr.openai.com , for example, is OpenAI's ad-measurement pixel, embedded in advertisers' sites, and is queried by devices that never use ChatGPT.

- Keep non-usage roles out of usage counts. auth , cdn , telemetry and web names can corroborate activity, but browsers prefetch them, and they are reached by people who never use the product.

- Count distinct devices per service per day or week, not queries. Caching, retries, background refresh and prefetching distort query counts.

- Classify the name the client asked for , not CDN alias (CNAME) targets in the response.

### Coverage gaps

DNS-based measurement misses:

- off-network devices;

- clients using encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) to outside resolvers;

- locally run models;

- AI features embedded in other SaaS products, which share the host application's hostnames;

- calls made from a vendor's backend.

Some services (OpenRouter, Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Vertex AI) front many models, and DNS cannot tell which model was used.

## Using it

Implement the matching rules above. For each pattern, a regex of ^ + the pattern with * replaced by .* (everything else escaped) + $ is enough. In Splunk, load the CSV as a lookup with match_type = WILDCARD(host_pattern) and max_matches = 1 .

On high-volume DNS indexes, filter on indexed terms before classifying: python3 scripts/splunk_terms.py prints a keyword filter that covers every pattern.

## Contributing

New services, endpoints and corrections are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md . Every change must pass python3 scripts/validate.py , which also runs automatically on pull requests.

# TenseMem

Memory that knows its tenses. Embedded, deterministic memory that AI agents can safely act on.

One SQLite file. No server required. The model proposes typed facts; the engine decides what is current.

pip install tensemem

from tensemem import FakeExtractor , Memory mem = Memory ( llm = FakeExtractor ()) mem . register_predicate ( "lives_in" ) added = mem . add ( "u1" , "I live in Delhi" ) ctx = mem . context ( user_id = "u1" , min_seq = added . seq , wait = 1.5 ) print ( ctx . text ) # fenced block the model can read print ( ctx . freshness . is_current ) # True once extract finished

FakeExtractor is rule-based and needs no API key. Same API with tensemem[openai] , tensemem[anthropic] , tensemem[ollama] , tensemem[litellm] , or Gemini ( GEMINI_API_KEY in the process environment).

## Why this exists

Similarity search returns both “I live in Delhi” and “I moved to Bangalore” and leaves the model to guess. TenseMem keeps one current value per slot, says whether the read is fresh, and refuses to learn from its own output.

- One current truth per ONE slot. A new city supersedes the old one. History still answers “where did I live before?”

- Every read reports freshness. as_of_seq , pending , is_current . Wait for a message, or see that it is not applied yet.

- No self-echo. Recalled context() is fenced. Extract needs a verbatim quote from the user.

- Corrections stick. correct() restores the displaced value and survives rebuild() with a newer model.

- The engine decides. The LLM emits typed ops. Deterministic rules apply them.

- No infrastructure. Default store is one SQLite file inside your process.

## Delhi, then Bangalore

mem . add ( "u1" , "I live in Delhi" ) mem . set ( user_id = "u1" , predicate = "lives_in" , value = "Bangalore" ) print ( mem . state ( "u1" ). values ) # {"lives_in": "Bangalore"} history = mem . history ( "u1" , predicate = "lives_in" ) # ACTIVE Bangalore, SUPERSEDED Delhi bangalore = next ( f for f in history . facts if f . object == "Bangalore" ) mem . correct ( bangalore . id ) # that move was never true print ( mem . state ( "u1" ). values ) # {"lives_in": "Delhi"}

flowchart LR E[episodes] --> X[extractor proposes ops] X --> R[resolver] R --> F[facts] F --> C["context() + freshness"] C -.->|fence stripped| X

Every surface is an adapter over Memory / AsyncMemory . The model proposes typed ops; resolve() decides mutations; apply() writes one SQLite file. Facts are a rebuildable projection of an append-only episode log.

# Tessary

Stop your agents from failing silently in production.

Docs · Self-host · Report an issue · Discussions

Tessary is an open-source reliability platform for AI agents in production. It monitors every trace, detects issues using cheap classifiers, groups related findings into cases, and investigates their root cause using trace and repository evidence.

## Get running

To try it without installing anything, sign up for Tessary Cloud at https://app.tessary.ai . It's free, needs no credit card, and its limits are on the pricing page .

To self-host, paste this into your coding agent:

Self-host Tessary for me by following https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary/blob/main/setup.md

setup.md is written as instructions to an agent: install what's missing, bring every service up, verify the frontend, and hand back the URL.

Prefer to run it yourself? The same install is one command, with nothing cloned and no .env to edit:

docker compose -f oci://docker.io/tessaryai/tessary:compose up -d -y

Either way, open http://localhost when docker compose -p tessary ps reports every service healthy. It needs Docker Engine 26 or newer and Docker Compose v2.34 or newer on the machine. Set up Tessary takes it from there.

Once it's running, instrument your agent so Tessary has traces to watch: see the instrumentation overview .

### 1. Point your agent's traces at it

Send OTLP traces to the endpoint shown during setup and add tessary.call_site.id to spans that invoke a model. Use instrument.md to have a coding agent identify and instrument these call sites.

### 2. Connect the repo (optional)

Connect a GitHub repository under Settings > Git integration and both triage and RCA cite the code that produced the failing traces.

## How it works

- Watch every trace. OTLP over HTTP and gRPC, and SDK push, normalize to the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* conventions at the edge. PII (personally identifiable information) redaction runs before storage.

- Filter cheaply. Classifiers sweep every trace continuously and open a finding when one fires. The per-trace check stays cheap enough to afford at production volume, which is what makes reading all of it possible instead of sampling. Two classifiers are exceptions, and both are off until you turn them on: frustration scores eligible user messages with a hosted model on your own OpenRouter or TypeSafe key, and groundedness checks answers against their retrieved documents with a public model you run on a Mac with Apple silicon or a GPU instance on AWS, not an LLM call.

- Group into cases. Related findings collapse into one case, surfaced on Triage . An LLM triage step rules whether a finding is a real deviation rather than a legitimate change, and only a finding it rules real becomes a case. Two kinds of finding are ruled when they are filed instead, because their numbers are the claim: a high-confidence secret leak, and a rise in frustrated conversations.

- Explain the case. RCA runs an agentic session over the failing traces and, when a repo is connected, the code itself. It returns a one-sentence summary, the causes it found with the traces behind each, and the checks it ruled out.

- Route it to a human. An alert carries the case to whoever owns it. Tessary explains and hands off. It doesn't open the fix.

## License

Tessary is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 .

## Telemetry

A self-hosted instance sends one anonymous heartbeat to home.tessary.ai at backend start and every 6 hours after. It carries a schema version, an install id, a ping sequence number, a timestamp, the edition, the app version, the host OS family and CPU architecture, install-wide totals of projects, ingested spans, findings, cases, and classifier detections, and the hash of the model price book it holds. On the same schedule it checks home.tessary.ai for a newer price book and downloads it only when the hash has changed. It never carries trace or prompt content, an email address, an org or project name, a hostname, or a retained IP address.

TESSARY_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false

Set that in .env and the instance makes no call to that host, DNS lookups included, and loses nothing: no feature, license check, or in-app behavior depends on the heartbeat reaching us. The field-by-field contract is the telemetry contract .

CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to open an issue or a pull request, how to run the checks locally, and what to expect from review. The documentation map is where to start reading the rest.

## Security

Report a vulnerability privately by emailing security@tessary.ai . See SECURITY.md for what to expect.

- Ask in words : type “warmer and a bit brighter”, “down exposure by ten points”, “shadows +25” or “paste the edits from the previous photo” (Ctrl/⌘ K). A small Rembrandt in dots thinks it over, then makes each change while you watch the sliders move. It runs on your device: a vocabulary, not a language model.

- Edit the photo itself : drag up or down on any part of the picture to lighten or darken that tone, left or right to change that colour; the sliders follow.

- AI looks : Enhance, Relight, Sky, Atmosphere, Sunrays, Skin, Motion and Lens Blur with aperture shapes, from on-device depth and subject maps.

- Refocus : brings back detail in out-of-focus photos, even heavy defocus (regularised deconvolution on the GPU), on the subject or the whole picture.

- Super Resolution : 2× and 4× with real detail, or Restore at the same size for soft photos; runs on the GPU (Metal on Apple silicon).

- AI Denoise : clean high-ISO shots into a new DNG with the same edits, on the GPU.

- Background work that stays out of the way : AI Denoise, Super Resolution and merges run in small GPU slices that pause while you edit, or when you're away, or overnight in a night window you set (Settings › Performance). The queue survives restarts.

- Merge : HDR from brackets, panoramas and focus stacks, each to a RAW-like DNG.

- RAW from 1,000+ cameras, developed on the GPU: tone, colour, curves, grading, dehaze, detail.

- Masks : brush, gradients, colour and tone ranges, AI subject, background, object and depth.

- Remove : heal and clone spots and strokes; Rembrandt picks a matching source for you.

- Lens corrections : the camera's built-in profile from Fujifilm and Sony RAWs, or one of 1,500 lens profiles from Lensfun (distortion, vignetting, chromatic aberration), plus manual distortion and vignetting for any photo. Auto straighten levels horizons.

- On-device AI : Refocus, background replacement. Nothing is uploaded.

- Library : albums, ratings, flags, colour labels, keywords, virtual copies, search, Find similar, sorting, keyboard shortcuts (or Lightroom's), one-click delete with Undo.

- Batch : copy and paste edits to hundreds of photos, batch export, and presets that fit each photo's exposure. Watch a folder to apply a preset and album to new photos as they arrive.

- Share how : a before/after page with a slider, a replay video of the edit, or the recipe inside the exported file so anyone can see (and reuse) how it was edited.

- Bring your photos : folders, Lightroom Classic (edits, keywords, labels, virtual copies, collections, with a report of anything that can't come over) and Lightroom, Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive ( setup ). Export back to them too.

- Open formats : edits are standard XMP, readable by Lightroom and others. Exports keep the camera details and date taken, add your name and copyright, and embed an sRGB profile; location is never written.

- Cloud sync (optional, paid) : turn it on in Settings to sync edits, albums and photos between your computers, the web and your phone. It's the only thing that needs an account, and the only thing that costs money; everything else stays free.

## How it compares

- Lightroom : the everyday editing and library work is here: RAW development, masks (including AI subject, depth and object), healing, presets, lens corrections, HDR and panorama merges, denoise, batch editing, and catalog import. Not here yet: Print, Book, Slideshow, Web and Map modules, face recognition, Adobe's camera profiles, tethered capture (a watched folder covers most tethering apps), and a plugin ecosystem.

- darktable : Rembrandt borrows darktable's central idea, a scene-referred pipeline (edits work on linear light before a tone curve maps it to the screen), which is why highlights recover cleanly. darktable has far more modules and control; Rembrandt aims to be usable in five minutes, with fewer, broader controls and on-device AI. The engine is an independent implementation (see Credits).

- RawTherapee / ART : similar ground to darktable; Rembrandt trades depth of control for speed of use.

- GIMP / Photoshop : different kind of tool. Those are pixel editors for compositing and painting; Rembrandt is a non-destructive RAW developer and library, like Lightroom.

## Your photos aren't locked in

Rembrandt never moves or rewrites your originals. Edits are saved as standard XMP sidecars next to your photos, which Lightroom, darktable and others can read, and Settings › Data & privacy exports a backup of all your edits. If Rembrandt disappeared tomorrow, your library and your edits would still be yours, in open formats.

## How it's built

JavaScript with WebGL2 and WebGPU shaders for the editing engine and on-device AI, in a small Rust ( Tauri ) desktop app. RAW files are decoded by LibRaw (C++, compiled to WebAssembly). Every release is built by GitHub Actions from this repository, with checksums and signed build provenance ( SECURITY.md ).

## Credits

- darktable : the scene-referred workflow Rembrandt's engine is modelled on. An early prototype ported darktable's algorithms; it was replaced by an independent implementation of the published methods (listed in NOTICE.md ) before the code was released.

- LibRaw (RAW decoding), Lensfun (lens profiles), RAWmakase (lens tables, heal and clone), Real-ESRGAN (Super Resolution), KAIR / FFDNet (AI Denoise), MediaPipe (subject, depth and object models). Licences and notices in NOTICE.md .

## Help out

Rembrandt is free and stays free. Star the repo, tell a photographer, report a bug or send a fix.

## Build

npm ci && npx http-server -c-1 . # web app npm run tauri dev # desktop app (Rust + Tauri prerequisites)

Details in docs/building.md . Contributions welcome: CONTRIBUTING.md .

# Veda: The Agentic-Native Operating System

Veda is an operating system with a voice agent built in. Say "Hey Veda, switch my wallpaper to the dunes" and it does the work in any application, through the same code as your keyboard and mouse. It asks you first before anything that is hard to undo.

The system is written in Rust and lives in this repository: the UEFI bootloader, a capability-based microkernel, the system services, the window system, the toolkit and the applications. Where a proven, widely used library exists, Veda uses it rather than its own: TCP/IP, TLS and cryptography (smoltcp, rustls, RustCrypto), image codecs (zune, qoi, fast_image_resize) and math (libm, glam, rand). Veda runs on x86-64 PCs and in QEMU.

## Why agentic-native

Operating systems were designed for a person at a keyboard. An assistant added later has to read the screen, imitate clicks or use the few applications that have an API, and the system cannot hold it to anything. In Veda, the agent is a first-class user of the system:

- Part of the system. The agent is a system service, started at boot and restarted if it fails. It sleeps until you say its name, click the ring on the taskbar or press Super+Space .

- Native in every application. Applications declare their actions (typed parameters and a risk level) and report what they show as JSON. The agent calls those actions, which run the same code as the keyboard and mouse: no screen scraping, no simulated clicks. The built-in applications offer more than 70 actions.

- Consent enforced by the system. Every action is routine , sensitive or destructive . The agent service, not the language model, holds the last two until you allow them. Only the desktop shell can answer ( init tells every service which program is calling), so nothing the agent reads in a document can approve anything.

- Real context. Each conversation starts with the time, the open windows, every application's actions, what the agent knows about you and how your last conversation ended. Before acting, it reads the applications' current state.

- Memory you control. It remembers only what you tell it plainly (your name, the people in your life, how you like things done), never its own guesses. The memory stays on your computer, and Settings shows and forgets any part of it.

- Voice first. You can interrupt it at any time. Echo cancellation and an echo gate keep it from hearing itself, and other sound drops 20 dB during a conversation. Asleep, it listens with a voice detector that runs locally, so no audio leaves the computer while nobody speaks.

- The intelligence is a setting. Speech recognition, the language model and the voice come from Deepgram's Voice Agent API, with the audio opted out of Deepgram's model improvement. The model (OpenAI's gpt-4.1-mini by default), the voice and even the agent's name are chosen in Settings.

## How the agent works

- Listening. Asleep, the agent runs a voice detector on the computer. Speech it hears goes to Deepgram's recogniser, with the agent's name as a key term. A sentence that starts or ends with the name ("Hey Veda, …", "…, Veda?") wakes the agent, and the rest of the sentence is its first request.

- Conversation. Waking opens a Deepgram Voice Agent session with the agent's instructions, context and functions. Deepgram handles turn-taking, the language model and the voice; Veda's audio service carries the sound both ways.

- Action. The model calls the agent's 17 functions (windows, files, volume, Wi-Fi, wallpaper, notifications, timers and reminders, memory, the system and its programs) and, through use_app and read_app , every application's actions and state. Each call returns a structured result.

- Consent. A call that needs your OK waits in the agent's window, or in a notification, saying exactly what will happen and to what. It runs only if you allow it within three minutes. Sensitive actions can be allowed for good; destructive ones are asked about every time.

The agent covers the design in full: the protocols, the voice pipeline, consent, memory and testing.

## The operating system

- Microkernel. vkernel handles only isolation, scheduling, memory and IPC: capability handles with rights, channels that carry messages and handles, VMOs, events, futexes and interrupt objects. It supports SMP with x2APIC, tickless timers and XSAVE.

- Supervised services. Drivers, the file system, the window system, audio, networking and the agent are user-space processes. init restarts the window system, the shell, audio, networking and the agent if they crash, so the desktop comes back on its own.

- Linux's drivers in a VM. Veda drives only its disks (virtio-blk, AHCI, NVMe). Linux drives everything else in the driver VM , on Veda's own hypervisor (VMX with EPT, no emulated hardware). Devices go to it whole, their DMA confined and their interrupts remapped by Veda's IOMMU driver. A crashed driver takes down only the VM, which Veda resets and restarts. See the driver VM .

- Desktop. A compositing window manager with server-side decorations, shadows, animations, snapping and an Alt+Tab switcher with live thumbnails. It composes on the GPU with Intel graphics and on the processor elsewhere; once Linux drives the display, every frame is flipped whole at the vertical blank. The shell has a taskbar, a searchable start menu, desktop icons, a calendar and notifications.

- Toolkit. vui is an immediate-mode toolkit: widgets, menus, dialogs, vector icons and anti-aliased text in Inter and JetBrains Mono. Every vui application is agent-compatible.

- 3D graphics. OpenGL ES 3.0 with GLSL ES 1.00 and 3.00, in Rust ( vgl , vglsl ), every call checked as the specification requires. It renders on the GPU through Mesa in the driver VM (Intel's iris; virgl on the host's GPU under QEMU), or on a multi-threaded software renderer. Interceptor shows it off, full screen: a bay city with its traffic, physically based lighting, shadows, bloom and 4x multisampling.

- Networking. A network service with IPv4 and IPv6, DHCP, DNS, TCP, UDP and ICMP, and a Wi-Fi service that joins WPA2, WPA3 and open networks with management frame protection, remembers them, reconnects and roams. Linux's drivers only move frames and never see a password. Applications get TLS 1.3 and 1.2 from vtls , with certificates checked against Mozilla's roots. See Networking .

- Audio. A mixing service with echo-cancelled recording and ducking, built for the agent's conversations as much as for music.

- Video. FFmpeg and dav1d, ported to Veda, decode the common formats (AV1, VP9, H.264, HEVC and more) in a sandboxed process that reaches nothing but the file it is given: a damaged file that crashes or hangs it costs a moment, not the video. Pictures come through shared memory and are shown in time with the sound, timed to the screen's refresh. See Architecture .

- Storage. The home directory has its own disk. It is saved half a second after changes stop, alternating between two checksummed slots, so an interrupted save never damages the previous one. The agent's memory and key live in a private directory that only the agent can open.

- C and GCC. The image includes GCC 16, binutils and musl: write a C program in the Terminal, compile it and run it, in QEMU or on a PC. C programs are static executables whose system calls go to vposix , a POSIX layer in Rust. A cross compiler also builds C and C++ programs for Veda on the development machine. See C on Veda .

## Applications

Every application is agent-compatible: what you can do with the mouse and keyboard, the agent can do too.

## Screenshots

Every screenshot is 1280x800. They are taken in QEMU by cargo xtask script docs/screenshots.vts , with the agent talking to a stand-in for Deepgram. Interceptor's is taken at 1920x1200 by cargo xtask script docs/interceptor.vts --resolution 1920x1200 and scaled down.

## Quick start

### Requirements

Veda is built on an x86-64 PC with Linux.

- Rust , stable. rust-toolchain.toml makes rustup install the extra targets on first use, and Rust's own linker ( rust-lld ) links everything.

- QEMU and the OVMF UEFI firmware (on Debian and Ubuntu: qemu-system-x86 , qemu-system-gui , qemu-system-modules-opengl and ovmf ), with access to /dev/kvm .

- For the driver VM: the build tools for Linux, a cross compiler and Mesa (on Debian and Ubuntu: build-essential , bc , curl , rsync , m4 , flex , bison , meson , ninja-build , libgmp-dev , libmpfr-dev , libmpc-dev , python3-mako and python3-packaging ), and KVM's nested virtualization ( kvm_intel nested=1 ). See the driver VM .

- Optional: a Deepgram API key for the agent, and your distribution's build tools for the C toolchain, which cargo xtask toolchain builds once (see C on Veda ), with nasm for the video decoders it builds too.

Check the environment:

cargo xtask doctor

### Build and run

First, build the driver VM's Linux (its kernel, a cross compiler and Mesa), which takes a while. Without it, Veda boots with no keyboard, mouse, sound or network.

cargo xtask linux

Then build and run Veda:

cargo xtask run

This builds every component, writes target/veda/veda.img and boots it in a QEMU window at 1920x1080. The first build also renders the sample pictures, music and videos. Later builds are incremental.

Videos plays videos with FFmpeg and dav1d, which the C toolchain builds (it needs nasm ). Build it once, and the images built after it include the decoder:

cargo xtask toolchain

cargo xtask run --resolution 1280x800 --smp 4 --memory 2048 cargo xtask run --cmdline " run=editor " cargo xtask run --net wifi

run=NAME starts /system/bin/NAME.exe after boot. By default the machine reaches the Internet through a wired card on QEMU's NAT. --net wifi gives it a Wi-Fi radio instead, and starts airsim , a simulated Wi-Fi environment whose networks ("Veda Home", "Veda WPA3", ...) lead to the Internet with the password veda-wifi ; --net both gives it both. cargo xtask help lists every command and option.

### A real PC, from a USB stick

cargo xtask iso

This writes target/veda/veda.iso , a live system. To start it:

# cliproxy-rs

Watch the launch film

## What is this?

cliproxy-rs is a small server you run on your own computer. It lets your coding tools, such as Claude Code, Codex CLI or Cursor, use the AI subscriptions and API keys you already have, like a Claude Max plan or a ChatGPT plan, through one local address. A dashboard built into it shows which accounts work, how much of each plan's limits is left, and how to connect each tool.

It is a Rust rewrite of CLIProxyAPI . It reads the same config.yaml and the same account files, so you can switch between the two in either direction.

## Why would I want it?

- You pay for Claude and ChatGPT plans and want Claude Code, Codex CLI and your editor to share them, with the 5-hour and weekly limits of every account on one screen.

- You have several Claude or Codex accounts and want requests spread across them, or moved to the next account when one reaches its limit.

- A tool speaks only one API: the proxy translates between the Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini formats, so an OpenAI-only tool can use a Claude account and the other way round.

- You run CLIProxyAPI and want a smaller, faster-starting binary with the dashboard built in.

## Quick start

- Run one command. On macOS or Linux: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vayungodara/cliproxy-rs/master/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / vayungodara / cliproxy - rs / master / install.ps1 | iex It installs the latest release after checking its checksum, writes a config with new keys to ~/.cliproxy-rs , starts the proxy in the background and opens the dashboard in your browser. The keys stay in ~/.cliproxy-rs/keys.env and are never printed.

Run one command. On macOS or Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vayungodara/cliproxy-rs/master/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / vayungodara / cliproxy - rs / master / install.ps1 | iex

It installs the latest release after checking its checksum, writes a config with new keys to ~/.cliproxy-rs , starts the proxy in the background and opens the dashboard in your browser. The keys stay in ~/.cliproxy-rs/keys.env and are never printed.

- In the dashboard, sign in with the CLIPROXY_MANAGEMENT_KEY line from keys.env and choose Connect account.

- Open Use with tools and copy the settings for Claude Code, Codex CLI or another tool.

Run the same command again to upgrade; your config and keys stay as they are. docs/INSTALL.md shows how to start the proxy when you log in.

docs/GETTING-STARTED.md walks through the same steps in more detail.

Using a subscription outside its official app can break the provider's terms, and providers have suspended accounts for it. Whether to do that is your call and your risk.

## Set up with an AI agent

Paste this into Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent on the computer where you want the proxy:

Install and set up cliproxy-rs on this computer by following https://github.com/vayungodara/cliproxy-rs/blob/master/docs/AI-SETUP.md exactly. Do not sign in to any of my accounts or print my keys; tell me when it is my turn.

The agent runs the installer, which picks a free port without touching an existing CLIProxyAPI and keeps the keys in a file only you can read. It checks that the proxy answers, then hands the account sign-in to you.

## Use it with your tools

The proxy serves the Anthropic Messages API at http://127.0.0.1:8317 , the OpenAI API at http://127.0.0.1:8317/v1 and the Gemini API at http://127.0.0.1:8317 , all with your client key. For Claude Code:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8317 export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=your-client-key claude

docs/CLIENTS.md has copy-paste setups for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Amp, OpenCode, Factory Droid, Cline, Roo Code, Kilo Code, Cursor, Zed, Continue, Aider and the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini SDKs.

## Several accounts

Sign in to as many Claude and Codex accounts as you have, and choose how the proxy rotates between them: round-robin , fill-first , weighted-round-robin , or soonest-reset (experimental, a cliproxy-rs addition: spend the account whose weekly window resets soonest first). Session affinity keeps each conversation on one account so the provider's prompt cache stays warm, and an account that hits a limit rests while the others take over. docs/MULTI-ACCOUNT.md covers routing, cooldowns, the quota view, per-account proxies, Codex over WebSocket and reaching the proxy from your other machines over Tailscale.

## Works with CLIProxyAPI apps

cliproxy-rs serves the same routes and the same v8 Management API as CLIProxyAPI, so the community apps built on CLIProxyAPI should work with it, for example CPA-Manager-Plus , CLIProxyAPI Quota Inspector , ZeroLimit , Quotio , VibeProxy and CCS . We have not tested all of them. Apps that talk to a running server need only its address and management key; apps that start their own bundled CLIProxyAPI need an option to use an existing server instead. If an app does not work with cliproxy-rs, please open an issue .

## Install options

- install.sh (macOS and Linux) and install.ps1 (Windows), the commands in the quick start. They install the release binary, set it up and start it; --binary-only ( -BinaryOnly on Windows) installs only the binary.

- Release binaries for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Linux (x86_64 and arm64) and Windows (x86_64), with a SHA256SUMS file, on the releases page .

- Docker, from the repository's Dockerfile .

- Building from source, for contributors and platforms without a release binary.

docs/INSTALL.md covers each one, starting the proxy at login, and removing it.

## Upcoming features

These are not in cliproxy-rs yet. They are planned, in no fixed order:

- Homebrew and AUR packages.

- Plugins: the host callbacks plugins use to call back into the server, calling plugins on the request path (plugin providers, sign-in, models and usage), and the plugin store. Today plugins load, serve their own routes and report quotas, but requests do not pass through them.

- Home (cluster) mode: reporting usage, logs and in-flight requests back to Home, Home's KV storage, and syncing plugins managed by Home.

- Google Antigravity.

- Image generation and editing through Codex accounts, and importing Vertex service accounts from the dashboard (the command line works).

- The terminal UI ( -tui ).

- The pprof debug listener.

- The upstream request and response sections of request log files.

- The rest of CLIProxyAPI's own test cases. The parity audit checked 1,687 Go routes, settings, flags and test suites: 798 (47%) are fully covered, 697 partly and 192 not yet. docs/PARITY.md explains the numbers.

- Getting started : install, configure, connect an account and a tool.

- Set up with an AI agent : exact steps a coding agent can follow.

- Use it with your tools : setup for each coding tool and SDK.

- Several accounts : routing, limits, quotas and remote access.

- Configuration : the settings you are most likely to change.

- Install : every install option, Docker and running as a service.

- Compatibility and parity and benchmarks .

## Security

Keep access.api-keys set and server.host on 127.0.0.1 unless you need other machines to connect. Behind a tunnel or reverse proxy on the same machine, set server.trusted-proxies , or every internet client counts as local. The dashboard is built into the binary, and cliproxy-rs never downloads code to run. Running it safely explains each point, and SECURITY.md says how to report a vulnerability.

## Performance

Go is faster on non-streaming throughput. On a 2-vCPU test machine with a local fake upstream (2026-10-03), CLIProxyAPI handled about 34% more non-streaming requests per second (1,568 against 1,168) and about 10% more plain streams (916 against 833). cliproxy-rs was faster on streams it translates between the Anthropic and OpenAI formats (793 against 564 per second, about 41% more) and used less than half of Go's memory: 17 MB at idle against 45 MB, and 25 to 50 MB under load against 58 to 104 MB. The workspace is crates/cpa-core (config and account formats), crates/cpa-exec (one module per upstream provider), crates/cpa-translate (format translation), crates/cpa-server (routes, account selection and the Management API), crates/cliproxy (the binary) and ui/ (the dashboard, see ui/README.md ).
