# Can AI draw San Francisco from memory?

In 2023, Gurnee and Tegmark showed that you can read the latitude and longitude of places straight out of a language model's activations. So there is a map in there somewhere. We wanted to see it.

We gave six AI models 41,526 points of San Francisco and asked what is at each one: water, a park, a building, a street or something else. They answered from memory, with no maps and no internet, and we checked every answer against OpenStreetMap.

The best models know San Francisco like a tourist with a good memory. They put the coastline, Golden Gate Park and the Presidio in the right place and get the street grid wrong. Paying five times more bought the same score, and thinking harder did not find the streets. Jev, a model from TypeSafe that we asked one point at a time, put the Marina underwater and was only 37% sure of its answers there.

The code, every answer and the answer keys are open. Three commands rebuild the scores, costs and figures without an API key ( run it yourself ).

Jump to: the whole city · the Marina · one block, medium against high · what broke · how precise this is

## What we asked

Every chat model got the same question, 100 points at a time, in random order:

> You are taking part in a map-knowledge test about San Francisco, California. Answer from your own knowledge only. Below are 100 locations in San Francisco, in no particular order, as WGS84 latitude, longitude: 1. 37.80241, -122.44853 ... For each location give one letter for what is at that exact spot: W = water (bay, ocean, lake or pond), P = park, lawn, trees or other green open space, H = inside a building, S = on a street (roadway or sidewalk), O = anything else (parking lot, plaza, beach or empty lot).

You are taking part in a map-knowledge test about San Francisco, California. Answer from your own knowledge only.

Below are 100 locations in San Francisco, in no particular order, as WGS84 latitude, longitude: 1. 37.80241, -122.44853 ...

For each location give one letter for what is at that exact spot: W = water (bay, ocean, lake or pond), P = park, lawn, trees or other green open space, H = inside a building, S = on a street (roadway or sidewalk), O = anything else (parking lot, plaza, beach or empty lot).

We tested two models from each of the big three, at low, medium and high reasoning:

We also asked two things that are not chat models, one point at a time: Jev by TypeSafe, and OpenAI's Decisions API, which runs GPT-6 Luna. Both answer a multiple-choice question and return a probability for each choice, so they seemed a natural fit for "which of these five is it?"

There are three maps:

- All of San Francisco, a point every 100 m. 15,846 points. At this spacing a point lands on a street or a building by chance, so we score it as water, park or everything else.

- Crissy Field, the Palace of Fine Arts and the Marina, a point every 10 m. 23,180 points and all five classes. We slid a box this size over the whole city, and of 236 positions this one has the 4th most even mix of water, parks, buildings and streets. We took it over the top three (Ocean Beach, Lands End and Hunters Point) because it puts Crissy Field, the Palace of Fine Arts and the Marina's grid in one box.

- A 500 x 500 m piece of the Marina street grid, a point every 10 m. 2,500 points at medium and at high reasoning, to see if more thinking finds the streets.

## San Francisco at 100 m

Right is the share of points with the right answer. mIoU is fairer when the classes are uneven: for each class, take the points where the model and the map agree and divide by the points where either of them says that class, then average over water, park and everything else. The table is sorted by mIoU.

Every model draws its best map at high reasoning. Gemini 4 Argon stays flat from low to medium, because it only starts reasoning at high. Claude Fable 5.1 costs the most at low and medium and lands behind the OpenAI models and Gemini 4 Argon on mIoU at every level.

At high reasoning, Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra are within a point of each other, which is a tie, and Astra costs five times more than the other two. GPT-6.1 Sol gets 83% at medium for $4.61.

Argon reached the top only after we re-sent the 4 of its 159 requests that came back empty. On denser maps it breaks much more often (see When the models broke ).

The good maps all have the coastline, Golden Gate Park, the Presidio and Lake Merced. Small parks are hit and miss: the best park score is 0.45. Jev draws a box, with water around the edge and everything else inside, which still beats answering "everything else" everywhere. The Decisions API calls 53% of the city a park.

## The Marina at 10 m

All five classes count here. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 put the Palace of Fine Arts lagoon in the right place, and Astra and Sol put the Palace building next to it. Fable draws the Marina's long east-west streets as stripes across the whole map.

Claude Opus 5.5 does not believe in streets. It calls 3% of the Marina a street, against 21% in reality, and paints the grid as one big building. That gets it the most points right and the lowest street score of any chat model.

Fable, Astra and Sol score 0.19-0.21 on streets here, against 0.11-0.14 if their own answers were shuffled at random. That looks like knowing which parts of the map are dense grid and which are park.

Jev puts the Marina underwater: 84% of its answers here are water. It was not sure, though. Jev gives a probability for each of the five answers, and the one it picked got 37% on average, against 20% for a blind guess. It was as sure of its wrong answers as of its right ones. The Decisions API's answers were split between water and park, and it was no different: 41% on average, right or wrong.

## Medium against high reasoning on one Marina block

To see whether the models know where single streets run, we took a 500 x 500 m piece of the Marina, 46% buildings and 33% streets, and asked every model at medium and at high reasoning.

High reasoning adds 0.01-0.03 to the street score and costs up to 3.6 times as much (Gemini 4 Argon aside: 48 times as much, for answers on 8% of the points). No model draws the grid at either level. The chance column shows what each model would score if we shuffled its own answers around the block, keeping how often it says "street". Only GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol beat that, by 0.04-0.09, which is a thin margin on 25 requests. Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5 and both Geminis score about what they would by putting the same number of streets in random places.

## When the models broke

Gemini 4 Argon thinks itself out of room. At high reasoning it thinks for about 15,000 tokens per request on the city map. On the dense Marina block it thinks for about 30,000, even when we send it only 10 points. Its output limit is 32,768 tokens, thinking included, so 10-point requests just fit. Redoing the block that way would have cost about $75, so we left the hole.

GPT-6.1 Sol at high can think for up to half an hour per request. After OpenAI's Batch API stalled, we sent the rest through the regular API, and 11 requests outlasted our 30-minute connection limit. OpenAI's background mode, which runs the request on their side and lets you check back later, finished all 11.

In early tests, models asked for 100 letters in a row sometimes wrote 90 or 101. So every answer is numbered ("17:H"), and a missing or extra letter cannot shift the rest.

Apart from Gemini 4 Argon high on the block, every run answered 100% of its points.

## How precise is this?

We ran GPT-6.1 Sol medium and Gemini 4 Argon low on the city map a second time. 12% and 11% of points changed between water, park and everything else (29% and 25% with all five classes), but the scores moved by less than half a point: 83.4% to 83.7% and 80.1% to 79.7%. So both scores held while single points flipped.

We also asked Jev and the Decisions API about every point a second time, to keep their probabilities. The Decisions API gave the same answers both times. Jev changed 9% of its answers on the city map and under 1% elsewhere, and its scores held.

The 95% ranges in results/summary.json come from resampling the requests. They are about ±0.5-0.8 points on the city map, so treat models within a point of each other as tied. On the small block they are about ±3 points.

OpenStreetMap is the answer key, so its mistakes count against the models. A point counts as a street if it is within 5-12 m of a street centreline, depending on the type of road. Freeways and footpaths do not count as streets, and private yards, parking lots and plazas land in "other".

Different wording, points in order instead of shuffled, or fewer points per request would change the numbers. Before this setup we asked for whole drawings of each block and for small grids of points. The drawings had seams where blocks met, and the grids came back with whole rows of the same letter, so we switched to shuffled points. We did not tune the setup on the scores.

## How we did it

- Points. A grid over each map, shuffled once with a fixed seed and cut into requests of 100 points. Jev and the Decisions API answer one point per request.

- Asking. Anthropic and OpenAI through their Batch APIs at half price, Gemini through the regular API. One try per request, except where the table above says otherwise: we asked empty Gemini 4 Argon high answers again (on the block we stopped after 24 retries in a row failed), and OpenAI requests a stalled batch never returned went through the regular API.

- Answer key. OpenStreetMap, downloaded on 18 October 2026. A point is water if it is in the sea, a lake or a pond; else a building if it is inside a building footprint; else a street if it is close to a street centreline; else a park; else other.

- Scoring. The share of points right, and mean IoU over the classes. A point with no answer stays out of "right" but lowers mIoU.

## Run it yourself

uv sync uv run python -m sfmap download # our answers and answer keys, into data/ uv run python -m sfmap score # results/summary.json uv run python -m sfmap figures # figures/ uv run pytest # tests

To ask the models yourself, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_KEY , then:

uv run python -m sfmap reference # download OpenStreetMap, build the answer keys uv run python -m sfmap run sf100 # or marina10, block10 uv run python -m sfmap collect # when the batches finish uv run python -m sfmap retry block10 argon high # re-send Gemini requests that came back empty uv run python -m sfmap background sf100 sol high # OpenAI requests a stalled batch never returned uv run python -m sfmap background sf100 sol medium --rerun # a whole second run uv run python -m sfmap references sf100 --rerun # Jev and the Decisions API again, with probabilities

## Who we are

We are VOYGR . We build APIs that tell AI agents which places exist, whether they are open and what they offer. This started as a quick question and got out of hand.

# Yana AI 🐰

Created by Vũ Văn Tâm · Vietnam

## Models propose. Yana decides. Humans stay in charge.

Yana is the control plane between an AI and real power. A model can say what it wants to do. Yana decides whether that is allowed, and a person can always stop it.

Model proposes an action | Authority is this agent allowed to ask? | Capability what exact power is this? (a small, fixed set) | Policy may it happen now? rules first, then a human | Executor performs only the permitted operation

Any model goes through the same path: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, or one running on your own machine. Skills teach an agent how to work; only a capability can grant permission to act.

## System structure

Live means shipped and in use. In development means real code exists but is not feature-complete. Experimental means opt-in and not independently verified.

yana-rt has 40 subcommands. Zero Python dependency. This is the source-defined count across feature builds, including feature-gated ones.

core/ ├── hooks/ # 66 PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop hooks (63 shell, 3 JavaScript) ├── rules/ # 71 rules, most are guidance the agent applies; hooks enforce a subset ├── agents/ # 100 specialist agents ├── skills/ # 2,026 skills ├── commands/ # 170 Claude Code slash commands └── config/ └── core-lock.json # SHA-256 manifest — 287 core files pinned

These counts are derived from the filesystem by core/scripts/check_counts.py , which CI runs, so they should not drift from the tree.

## Yana Studio

One window for the things you switch between when working with AI on a project. Studio talks to the model only through yana-rt ; it never calls a provider from the UI layer.

- Files and editor: open a real folder, search filenames across it, edit with CodeMirror. Files up to 8 MiB are editable; larger ones open as read-only 256 KiB windows. Saves detect outside changes before overwriting.

- Terminals: real PTY sessions in tabs, or a grid of up to 12.

- Git: read-only status, worktrees and diffs. Stage and commit are deliberately not AI tools.

- Chat: streamed through yana-rt , multiple saved conversations, stop button, approval prompts, token usage.

- Models: all 19 providers (13 cloud, 6 local) plus a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint. A local manager detects 9Router, Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, TurboFieldfare and AirLLM. API keys go to Rust over stdin and are stored encrypted with the OS keystore, never in workspace files.

- Tasks: create, list, depend and drop tasks against the real yana-rt task store. Marking done requires evidence, and blocked is always computed by the runtime.

- Design canvas: native canvas with 22 components, phone and desktop screens, layers, undo/redo, and guarded AI proposals.

- Governance telemetry: what was allowed, what was blocked, and why.

Not built yet: device registry, agent sessions screen, mobile pairing, SSH/Docker execution, permission-lease UI, signed auto-update. The per-screen status is in tools/yana-studio/SCREEN-STATUS.md .

Download from the latest release or yana.vutam.link .

Each release lists its own assets, so check that your platform is there, and verify against SHA256SUMS when provided. There is no Linux ARM build. The macOS build is ad-hoc signed and not notarized (no Apple Developer membership yet), so Gatekeeper warns on first launch; docs/MACOS_INSTALL.md shows the two official ways to open it.

Build from source (Node 24+ and a C++ toolchain for node-pty ):

cd tools/yana-studio npm ci && npm run rebuild npm run stage:runtime -- /absolute/path/to/yana-rt npm start

## Runtime: yana-rt

A single Rust binary that owns the turn loop and the authority check for every client, so Studio, the CLI and MCP do not each reimplement permission logic.

- 19 providers: anthropic, openai, gemini, groq, deepseek, openrouter, xai, novita, nvidia, minimax, glm, huggingface, 9router, kimi (cloud), and ollama, lmstudio, llamacpp, turbofieldfare, airllm (local). The canonical list is src/model/catalog.rs ; a contract test keeps Studio in sync with it.

- Failover: typed provider errors, fallback providers and credential-pool rotation.

- State: SQLite session store with full-text search, per-profile state, crash recovery, and shadow-git checkpoints with rollback.

- Capability tools: file read/patch, command execution under validation, MCP client over stdio, web.search through a checked HTTPS layer, and a read-only LSP client.

- Optional features: mcp , lsp , pty-bridge , Discord remote adapter. They are off in the default build.

Remaining work on the runtime is tracked in CURRENT-MILESTONE.md . At the time of writing: unifying every client on one capability executor, and running local-model tool calling against a real local model rather than a mock.

## Giám Thị

An independent watcher that runs outside any AI session, from the operating system's own scheduler: launchd on macOS, a systemd timer on Linux, Task Scheduler on Windows, every 6 hours.

- It compares the repo against a baseline commit a human approved, over the files that control enforcement: hook settings for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, CI workflows, core/rules , core/gates , core/hooks , core/scripts and src/guard .

- On drift it writes GIAMTHI_HALT.lock . A hook that runs first on every tool call then denies everything while the lock exists.

- Only a person deleting the lock clears it. Neither the hook, the watcher nor any environment variable can.

- Manage it with yana-ai giamthi install | status | repair | uninstall .

It is opt-in. Because it runs on a schedule, there is a window of up to 6 hours between a change and the halt. Codex fires PreToolUse only for shell commands, so Yana also checks the lock on SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit for Codex.

## Harness adapters

Details and switching commands: adapters/README.md .

## Command line

pip install yana-ai # Python CLI yana-ai install # add Yana's hooks and rules to your repo yana-ai doctor . # check that everything is wired cargo install yana-rt # native runtime, no Python needed

Needs Python 3.11+ (or Rust), Git, and one supported harness. All CLI commands are in COMMANDS.md . The 170 Claude Code slash commands ( /plan , /verify , /code-review and others) live in core/commands/ and run inside a session. Yana is not published to npm, see VERSIONING.md .

## What protects you, and where it stops

- Audit log: hash-chained, so editing or deleting a line is detectable ( core/scripts/verify-audit-chain.sh ). It is tamper-detectable, not tamper-proof.

- Core-lock: a SHA-256 manifest detects changed, deleted or injected files in core/ . It proves the tree matches the lock file, not that a human reviewed the change: whoever can edit core/ can also regenerate the lock. Giám Thị is the independent check for that.

- Human gate: force-push, publish, deploy and delete need confirmation in the current session; earlier approval does not carry over.

- Giám Thị: opt-in, runs outside any AI session, and on a finding locks every later tool call until a person removes the lock. It is periodic, not instant.

- Rules versus hooks: most files in core/rules describe behaviour the agent applies to itself. Only what is wired into a hook is enforced. There is no code-signing pipeline.

- Limits: guard-destructive.sh matches command strings, not a full shell parse, so a deliberately crafted command can slip past it. Antigravity is advisory, and Cursor does not screen MCP calls. Browser-only web deployments without the Rust runtime are not fully governed. Details: known limitations .

## Versioning

Three axes, each with its own number and registry: the product (not distributed), yana-rt on crates.io, and the yana-ai Python package on PyPI. Apps under tools/ ship through GitHub Releases with their own tags ( studio-v* for Studio). The numbers are deliberately not repeated here, since they go stale. See VERSIONING.md .

## More

ARCHITECTURE.md · PHILOSOPHY.md · ROADMAP.md · CURRENT-MILESTONE.md · CHANGELOG.md · CONTRIBUTING.md · SECURITY.md · Acknowledgements · Lineage

# Zephium

A fast, fully featured browser and work environment, reimagined for you and your agents.

Website · Docs · Launch film · Download

Safari's efficiency. Brave's protection. Arc's design. And Work , a canvas where your agents do real work in plain sight.

▶ Watch the launch film

Zephium is an open-source browser built in Rust on your operating system's own web engine: WebKit on macOS, the engine Safari uses, and WebView2 on Windows. It is not a fork of Chromium or Firefox. It blocks ads and trackers natively, runs Chrome extensions, and puts tasks, notes and your time on the web one click away. The download is about 30 MB.

One switch away is Work . Your work already happens in the browser, where your tabs, logins and history are. Work brings agents there instead of asking you to move somewhere else, and lets you watch them do it.

## Work

Describe an outcome in your own words: plan a trip, compare vendors, design a system, fix a bug. Work takes it from there on a canvas, and you see every step.

Asked for a status page, Work reads three monitors on their own sites, checks your endpoints from your machine, builds the pick, and leaves the comparison, the config and the tasks on the canvas.

- It starts from what you already have. Work recalls what it knows about you, searches your history when it helps, and loads the right skill for the job. Each step appears on the canvas as it happens.

- Helpers work in parallel, in the open. For a trip, one helper looks for flats while another checks visas and a third compares flights. They browse live pages you can watch, and any source opens in a pane beside the canvas.

- Results stay on the canvas. Comparisons, tables, charts, diagrams, plans, code and documents are laid out where you can read them. They are not lost in a chat scroll.

- A plan becomes your day. One click turns each step of a plan into a task linked back to the Work. Anything worth keeping can be saved as a note.

- It reaches past the browser. Work reads and edits the folders you grant, runs commands, and hands larger coding jobs to Claude Code or Codex. It connects to MCP servers such as Linear, Notion, Sentry, Stripe and Figma, and to command-line tools such as gh .

- You stay in charge. Anything that posts, merges or changes something waits for your OK.

- Bring any model. Use your own keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, xAI, Mistral, DeepSeek, Groq, Cerebras or OpenRouter, or run a model locally through Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible server. Keys live in your system keychain. Or sign in to Zephium AI and skip the keys: it picks the right model for each step, and you start with free credits ( pricing ).

Work ships with 25 skills, including trip planning, research, compare and choose, plan my day, fix a bug and weekly status. You can write your own.

## Ask Zephium

An assistant in the sidebar, on ⌘ E ( Ctrl E on Windows). It reads the page you are on and answers about it, points at what is worth your time, and opens what you choose in new tabs. Ask it to take a few steps on the page, or to restyle a site you visit every day, and it does it in place. When a job outgrows a chat, Continue in Work carries it to the canvas, with the page along.

Asked what is worth reading, it picks three stories, opens them, and re-sets the front page as calm cards.

## Browse

### Fast and light

- Native WebKit on macOS and WebView2 on Windows, so pages run on the engine your system already keeps up to date.

- Inactive tabs go to sleep and wake when you return, so memory stays low with many tabs open.

- A native ad and tracker blocker, on by default, built on Brave's adblock-rust with EasyList and EasyPrivacy. Requests are stopped before a page can make them, and you can hide anything else on a page with a click.

### Designed to live in

- A new tab that opens onto the sky, by day or by night with your theme, with your time, your focus and the day's tasks along its foot.

- Vertical tabs in a quiet sidebar, with spaces, profiles, pinned tabs, folders and split view.

- Liquid Glass on macOS 26 and Mica on Windows 11.

- A launcher on ⌘ ⇧ Space ( Ctrl Shift Space on Windows) reaches tabs, history, notes and commands from anywhere on your desktop. Anything you type there can become a task.

- Every keyboard shortcut can be changed.

### Extensions

Install extensions straight from the Chrome Web Store. Twenty popular ones are verified to work well in Zephium and are a click away in the extension manager, including 1Password, Bitwarden, Grammarly, DeepL, Dark Reader, Vimium, SponsorBlock, Raindrop.io, Notion Web Clipper and Refined GitHub.

### Bring everything with you

The welcome flow imports from Chrome, Safari, Arc, Zen, Firefox, Brave and Edge.

## Built in

## Private by default

- No telemetry. Zephium doesn't collect or send anything about how you browse.

- No account needed. History, tasks, notes, memory and time live on your device. An account is only for Zephium AI, and until you sign in, Zephium never contacts our servers.

- Zephium AI keeps no content. Requests pass through to the model that answers them. We count usage for your plan, never store prompts, answers or pages, and never see your card.

- Private windows keep nothing once they close.

## Download

Windows builds are not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may show "Windows protected your PC". Choose More info , then Run anyway . Signing is on the way.

Zephium downloads updates in the background and installs them when you choose Relaunch to update . All releases are on the releases page .

## What's next

- Linux and Intel Macs.

- Code-signed Windows builds.

- More extensions verified to work, and native extensions built into Zephium.

- And much more.

## Build from source

Prerequisites:

- Rust through rustup . The toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml installs itself on first use.

- Node.js, at the version in .node-version .

- pnpm, through Corepack: corepack enable .

- The Tauri prerequisites for your platform: Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS, or the Microsoft C++ Build Tools and WebView2 on Windows.

git clone https://github.com/zephium-browser/Zephium.git cd Zephium pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm dev

Development builds use their own app.zephium.dev profile, so they do not touch the data of an installed Zephium. Linux is not supported yet. See CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request.

## Architecture

- Untrusted pages run in raw native WebViews, apart from the privileged Svelte interface that draws the browser.

- A Rust core owns tabs, storage, the blocker, extensions and agents.

- Each profile has its own isolated website data and Zephium-owned history, session and favicon data.

- The network blocker is native and built on Brave's adblock-rust .

- Narrow in-tree adapters for Tauri and Wry handle storage policy, WebView construction, callbacks and teardown.

Zephium is maintained by one person with a clear product direction, so please discuss larger changes before writing them. CONTRIBUTING.md explains what gets merged and how. Questions and ideas are welcome on Discord .

# Unterm

The terminal AI agents can drive.

If Unterm is useful to you, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other people find it.

Cross-platform terminal (macOS / Linux / Windows) built on Unterm's native next-core terminal engine, with one design bet: the terminal itself is controllable from the outside by any AI agent over MCP. Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Aider, your own scripts — they all get the same JSON-RPC surface ( 152 authenticated methods plus auth.login ) to spawn shells, run commands, read pane state, capture screenshots, record sessions, and run the Agent Cockpit. (Theme, language and unterm.conf are not on MCP; they are set through Web Settings, unterm-cli , or the file.)

Since v0.68 the terminal is also something an orchestrator can govern rather than merely call: it publishes what it can do and how dangerous each capability is, works under leases that expire and cannot be replayed, keeps agents inside workspaces that cannot see each other, and can hand you an evidence bundle for a task that somebody who was not there can verify.

Since v0.55 the relationship runs both ways: agents drive the terminal from outside, and the terminal is an Agent Cockpit for the agents running inside it — live per-pane agent state, a waiting-first Inbox, fleets of N agents on one task in N isolated git worktrees, and a Review page to diff / merge / roll back what they produced.

The other 2026 terminals each pick a different side: Warp embeds AI inside a closed cloud (Oz), Ghostty stays out of your way and lets you bring your own tools, iTerm2 is Mac-only. Unterm picks the third side — terminal as MCP-controllable surface, deliberately keep AI generation out of the terminal, let external agents grip it through the API, and give the human one cockpit to run them all from.

Practical implications:

- Every Unterm window starts a local MCP server (line-delimited JSON-RPC over TCP) and a local HTTP settings server (Web Settings page) on auto-allocated ports. Both are auth-token gated, both are 127.0.0.1-only, no cloud round trip.

- Settings live in the browser , not the terminal. Cell-grid TUIs can't deliver modern form UX (no proper text inputs, no live preview, no color picker). The in-terminal ▼ menu holds quick actions and links out to the Web Settings page — configuration itself happens in the browser.

- 9 languages out of the box : en / 简体中文 / 繁體中文 / 日本語 / 한국어 / Deutsch / Français / Italiano / हिन्दी. Auto-detects from system locale, can be overridden in Web Settings or via unterm-cli lang set <code> .

- Multi-instance discovery : every running Unterm process owns one NATO-named instance (alpha, bravo, charlie…) and writes its ports + auth token to ~/.unterm/instances/<name>.json . Agents that drive several windows at once enumerate that directory.

- Cross-platform parity is a correctness property : if a feature works on Windows but bails on macOS or Linux, that's a bug, not "not supported yet."

- Subtraction over decoration : no AI chat overlay inside the terminal and no cloud dependency for core operation. Proxy settings auto-detect the system by default and also support explicit HTTP/SOCKS overrides, node pools, rotation, and Clash/mihomo controllers. Finder integration on macOS uses the native Finder right-click extension and Services.

The GUI and terminal runtime now use Unterm's native next-core engine. The repository still carries selected upstream components and attribution where they remain dependencies, but WezTerm mux/window state is no longer the product kernel.

## Agent Cockpit

Run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, or Aider in any pane and Unterm sees them — no configuration, no wrapper. Five pillars, all local:

- Agent state engine — every pane's agent and its state (working / waiting-for-you / idle / done), read from OSC progress + title signals, process fingerprints, and optional official hooks. Tab badges + a cross-window tally chip in the top bar.

- Inbox ( Ctrl+Shift+A ) — every agent that's waiting for you in one queue, longest-waiting first. Enter jumps to the pane; one keystroke later you've answered its prompt.

- Fleet — one task × N agents × N isolated git worktrees ( ../<repo>.fleet/ ), one tab each. Same agent ×3 for throughput, or claude,codex,gemini for a bake-off.

- Review — agents get checkpointed before they touch a repo (dangling-commit snapshots; nothing touches your HEAD or index). A Web Review page shows per-member diffs with squash-merge (stops at staged — the commit stays yours), discard, and rollback. Since v0.57, Review also verifies each member (inferred or explicit validation command), ranks members by verification + change size, gates merge on a passing run, and can retry a failed member in its existing worktree.

- Everything scriptable — the cockpit itself is MCP + CLI: agent.status , cockpit.inbox , fleet.launch , review.merge … an orchestrating agent can run fleets and review diffs with no human in the chair.

unterm-cli agent status # who's running where, in what state unterm-cli agent inbox # who's waiting for you unterm-cli agent enable-hooks # exact state via official hooks (merge-only, backed up) unterm-cli fleet launch --agents claude,codex " fix the flaky auth test " unterm-cli review verify --fleet < id > --member 1 # run the member's validation unterm-cli review list && unterm-cli review open # ranked diffs in the browser

Full docs: unterm.app/docs/agent-cockpit .

## Install

Pre-built artifacts are published on GitHub Releases:

https://github.com/zhitongblog/unterm/releases

### macOS

Double-click Unterm-macos-<version>.dmg , then drag Unterm.app onto the Applications shortcut. The DMG is signed with a Developer ID and Apple- notarized, so Gatekeeper opens it on first launch without warnings.

Finder integration is bundled in the DMG. After the first launch, Finder's right-click menu can show Open in Unterm for folders and files; if macOS doesn't refresh the extension immediately, run Repair Finder Integration.app from the DMG once.

### Linux (Debian / Ubuntu)

sudo apt install ./unterm- < version > .deb unterm

Other distros — use the AppImage:

chmod +x Unterm- < version > -x86_64.AppImage ./Unterm- < version > -x86_64.AppImage

### Windows

Run the MSI installer; it places unterm.exe in Program Files\Unterm and creates a Start Menu shortcut.

## What's new

- v0.68 — A terminal something else can govern. Unterm now hosts CLI agents as sessions rather than shelling out and waiting for an exit code ( agent_session.* : what it said, what it asked to run, how it ended, with your own task ids carried through untouched). It can lease a browser from Unzoo and be leased from in turn — terminal.manifest publishes what this terminal can do and how dangerous each family is, taken from the same table the gateway refuses by. Approvals can finally be answered: Settings shows what an agent is waiting on, with "allow once / for this task / always". Workspaces are roots that cannot see each other, and a shell that cd s out stops being inside. The audit trail is hash-chained, so an edit to it disagrees with the next line. unterm-cli provider | scope | artifact | evidence | system — 46 new MCP methods (149 total at the time; 152 today).

- v0.57 — Fleet verification loop + new brand mark. Review now verifies each fleet member automatically (Cargo / Go / npm / pnpm / yarn / Python / Maven / Gradle / .NET inferred, or your own command), ranks members by verification and change size, gates squash-merge on a passing run (audited force override), and retries failed members in their existing worktree without losing work — review.verify / fleet.retry over MCP + CLI. The sidebar gains repository-grouped navigation with always-on fuzzy search. Every logo surface moves to the new command-loop mark.

- v0.55 — Agent Cockpit. The terminal now sees the agents inside it: live per-pane state with tab badges and a cross-window tally, the waiting-first Agent Inbox ( Ctrl+Shift+A ), fleets running one task across N agents in N isolated worktrees, and a Review page with checkpoints, diffs, rollback, and squash-merge. 12 new MCP methods, 3 new CLI families.

- v0.54 — 2.8× faster cold start (~780ms → ~280ms) via five startup-path wins, and no more CPU core burned on Windows output floods (~91% → ~4%); MCP stays responsive mid-flood.

- v0.53 — Composer + Git panel. A prompt queue ( Ctrl+Shift+J ) that runs batched prompts into an agent pane with smart auto-advance through confirmation prompts, and a read-only Git status panel ( Ctrl+Shift+G ).

- v0.52 — More agents out of the box. Kimi Code CLI and Trae Agent join the baked manifest (7 agent CLIs total); reworked per-frame paint paths; steadier Windows clipboard and window sizing.

## Documentation

The full Unterm docs live at https://unterm.app/docs/ :

- Agent Cockpit — agent state engine, Inbox, Fleet, Review: run and supervise CLI agents from one terminal

- Agent integration — how to drive Unterm from Claude Code / Cursor / Aider / your own client

- Agent recipes — copy-paste patterns for common agent-drives-terminal workflows

- Product roadmap — what is being built now and what comes later

- Product requirements — complete product scope, functional requirements, MCP/CLI coverage, and acceptance criteria

- Detailed product planning — Chinese execution plan covering user scenarios, version roadmap, priorities, validation, and next-core migration

- Next-core product plan — staged plan to stabilize the current engine while building Unterm's own terminal core

- Next-core technical architecture — Chinese architecture plan for replacing the WezTerm core without growing into a larger terminal monolith

- MCP reference — every JSON-RPC method, parameters, return shape

- Multi-instance — NATO names, instances directory, picking the right window

- Identity profiles — one window per identity. Bind GitHub / AWS / npm / OpenAI tokens, git identity, SSH key routing all at once. CLI + MCP.

- CLI reference — unterm-cli subcommands, flags, exit codes

- Configuration — every file under ~/.unterm/

# More Space

A chalkboard and an avatar for any terminal agent. It shows its plan, its progress and its questions while it works.

## What it is

More Space is a desktop app with a real terminal floating over an endless chalkboard. Run any agent in that terminal (Claude Code, Codex, or anything else that can run shell commands) and it finds a command there that lets it:

- write and draw on the board: text, checklists, flow diagrams, pinned notes and photos, chalk links between them, circles, underlines and scribbles;

- be someone : an avatar you choose from a cast of characters, each with its own moods, look and voice;

- ask you things : choices, several answers, written answers or a scale, right on the board, and wait for your click;

- steer what you see : frame what it is explaining, or the whole board.

The command exists only inside the app's terminals and talks only to the window that opened them. Nothing is installed in your system, and nothing is written into your project.

## Getting started

- Download the app for your system from Releases (macOS: .dmg for Apple silicon or Intel; Windows: the Setup .exe ; Linux: .AppImage or .deb ).

- Open it and choose a project folder.

- The empty board shows a short instruction with a Copy button. Paste it to your agent in the terminal below; it will start by learning the board.

### Unsigned builds

Builds are not signed yet. The first time:

- macOS : open it once; when macOS says it is from an unidentified developer, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway (on older macOS, right-click the app and choose Open ). Or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/More Space.app" . The 0.1.0 build says "damaged" instead: it was not signed at all; the command above opens it.

- Windows : SmartScreen may warn about an unknown publisher; choose More info , then Run anyway .

## What the agent can do

Everything starts from the command with no arguments; each level explains the next, and more-space --all lists everything at once. more-space guide explains the board in one screen.

Several commands can go in one call, one per line: more-space - <<'EOF' … EOF in a Unix shell, or @' … '@ | more-space - in PowerShell. Every write answers with the cells it really covers, and warns when it lands on something else.

The avatar also lives along by itself:

- the terminal : busy while the program keeps printing, "Done" when it goes quiet, and calling you when the program rings the bell or sends a notification;

- the branch : it notices files changing as git sees them (an edit, a new or deleted file, an undone edit, a commit) and reacts in its own moods. Ignored files, like dependencies and builds, never count.

## Characters, sound and handwriting

- Characters : Mochi (the default, a plump pixel spirit), Chalky, Penguin, Owl, Robot, Cat, Cowboy, Samurai, Viking, Astronomer and Anime Hero. Each has its own moods (the agent reads them with avatar info ), drawing and voice.

- Sound : chalk on slate as it writes, a bell for questions. The character's own voice speaks only when it needs you ("Done", "Your turn in the terminal"); "Speak on every mood", in the character gallery, makes it speak on every mood the agent gives it too. One button turns all sound off.

- Handwriting : six chalk-like fonts; Patrick Hand by default.

### When an agent says the command is not found

Some tools keep one background process alive and run commands through it: tmux, screen, or Codex's shared app-server. That process keeps the environment of the terminal it was first started from. If it was started outside More Space, it cannot see the command: restart it once from a More Space terminal (for Codex: codex app-server daemon restart , or run codex --no-daemon ). Started from any More Space terminal, it keeps working afterwards, even across windows and restarts: the command lives in a fixed folder and finds the window open on the project it runs in.

## Your data

Boards are kept per project folder in the app's own data folder (on macOS, ~/Library/Application Support/more-space/boards/ ), never in the project. Pinned images are copied there. Nothing leaves your computer, except an image the agent pins from a URL, which the app downloads.

## Platforms

macOS, Windows and Linux. The terminal runs your login shell on macOS and Linux, and PowerShell on Windows (PowerShell 7 when installed, otherwise Windows PowerShell). Git must be installed for the branch in the title and for the avatar's reactions to file changes.

Needs Bun .

bun install bun start # build and open (asks for a project) bun start -- --cwd=/path/to/project # open straight on a project bun run check # typecheck, tests, build bun run package # installable app for this system, in release/ bun run icon # regenerate icon files from assets/icon/icon.svg

The project name is defined once, in package.json ; the window title, the command, the socket variable, the data folder and the packaged app's name all derive from it.
